playbooks.title: 502 Bad Gateway right after a deploy
playbooks.summary: Users get 502s for a minute or two every time you release, then it recovers.
playbooks.symptoms:
- Spike of 502 in nginx/ALB logs during each rollout
- `upstream prematurely closed connection` or `connect() failed (111)` in nginx error log
- Pods restarting or not Ready during the window
playbooks.causes:
- New pods get traffic before the app is ready (no or weak readiness probe)
- Old pods are killed while still serving (no graceful shutdown)
- `maxUnavailable` > 0 with few replicas
- Keep-alive: the app closes idle connections before the proxy does
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
kubectl -n prod rollout status deploy/web
kubectl -n prod get pods -w
kubectl -n prod describe pod <new-pod> | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Events/p'
grep -E 'upstream|connect\(\)' /var/log/nginx/error.log | tail
kubectl -n prod get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy}'
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Add a real readiness probe (an endpoint that checks the app can serve).
2. `maxUnavailable: 0`, `maxSurge: 1`, at least 2 replicas.
3. Graceful shutdown: `preStop: sleep 10` and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40`, app drains in-flight requests.
4. Make the app's keep-alive timeout longer than the proxy's (`keepalive_timeout` / ALB idle timeout).
playbooks.prevent:
- Watch 5xx during every deploy (deploy marker on dashboards)
- Canary or progressive rollout with automatic rollback on error rate
- Load test the rollout in staging

playbooks.title: CI pipeline got twice as slow
playbooks.summary: Builds that took 8 minutes now take 20+ and nobody changed the pipeline.
playbooks.symptoms:
- Build stage time doubled
- Dependency install or Docker build re-downloads everything
- Queue time grows (agents busy)
playbooks.causes:
- Docker layer cache lost (new runner, cache key changed, `COPY . .` before dependency install)
- Dependency cache key includes a timestamp or lockfile churn
- Fewer agents / shared runners saturated
- Tests grew without parallelism
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
# compare stage timings between a fast and slow run in the CI UI
docker history <image> --no-trunc | head -20     # which layers rebuild
git log --oneline -- Dockerfile requirements.txt package-lock.json | head
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Order the Dockerfile: copy lockfiles → install deps → copy code.
2. Use BuildKit cache (`--cache-from`/`--cache-to` registry cache) or Kaniko `--cache=true`.
3. Cache dependency dirs keyed on the lockfile hash.
4. Split tests into parallel jobs; run slow suites nightly.
playbooks.prevent:
- Track pipeline duration as a metric and alert on regressions
- Keep a prebuilt base image for heavy toolchains

playbooks.title: Build server disk full (Docker)
playbooks.summary: Builds fail with `no space left on device` on a CI or Docker host.
playbooks.symptoms:
- `no space left on device` in build logs
- `df -h` shows `/` or `/var/lib/docker` at 100%
playbooks.causes:
- Dangling images and build cache from every build
- Old containers and volumes never removed
- Huge container logs (json-file driver without rotation)
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
df -h; df -i
docker system df -v | head -40
sudo du -sh /var/lib/docker/* | sort -h
sudo find /var/lib/docker/containers -name '*-json.log' -size +500M -exec ls -lh {} +
```
playbooks.fix:
```bash
docker builder prune -af --filter until=72h
docker image prune -af --filter until=168h
docker container prune -f && docker volume prune -f
# rotate container logs: /etc/docker/daemon.json
# { "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "50m", "max-file": "3" } }
sudo systemctl restart docker
```
playbooks.prevent:
- Scheduled prune job on build hosts
- Disk usage alert at 80%
- Ephemeral build agents (fresh per job)

playbooks.title: helm upgrade stuck in pending-upgrade
playbooks.summary: A deploy timed out and now every `helm upgrade` fails with "another operation is in progress".
playbooks.symptoms:
- `Error: UPGRADE FAILED: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress`
- `helm status` shows `pending-upgrade`
playbooks.causes: - Previous upgrade was killed (pipeline timeout, cancelled job) before Helm wrote the final state
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
helm -n prod status web
helm -n prod history web
kubectl -n prod get secret -l owner=helm,name=web
```
playbooks.fix:
```bash
helm -n prod rollback web <last-deployed-revision>
# or, if rollback is not possible, mark the stuck release secret as failed:
kubectl -n prod get secret sh.helm.release.v1.web.v<N> -o yaml   # inspect first
helm -n prod upgrade web ./chart --install --atomic --timeout 10m
```
playbooks.prevent:
- Use `--atomic --timeout` so failed upgrades roll back cleanly
- Make the pipeline timeout longer than Helm's timeout

playbooks.title: Config change not picked up by pods
playbooks.summary: You updated a ConfigMap or Secret but the app still uses the old value.
playbooks.symptoms: - Old value in app behaviour or `/proc/1/environ`
playbooks.causes:
- Env vars from ConfigMaps/Secrets are read only at container start
- Mounted files update (after ~1 min) but the app caches them
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
kubectl -n prod get cm app-config -o yaml
kubectl -n prod exec deploy/web -- printenv | grep FEATURE_
```
playbooks.fix:
```bash
kubectl -n prod rollout restart deploy/web
# Helm: add a checksum annotation so config changes roll pods automatically
# annotations:
#   checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
```
playbooks.prevent:
- Checksum annotations in charts
- Reloader controller for automatic restarts on config change

playbooks.title: A secret was pushed to Git
playbooks.summary: An API key, password or cloud key ended up in a commit (maybe a public repo).
playbooks.symptoms:
- Secret scanner / GitHub push protection alert
- Unknown activity in cloud logs
- Someone spots `AKIA…` or a password in a diff
playbooks.causes: - Hard-coded credentials, `.env` committed, debug output pasted in code
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
gitleaks detect --source . --redact -v | head
git log -p -S 'AKIA' --all | head
# AWS: what did the key do?
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=AKIA... --max-results 50
```
playbooks.fix:
1. **Revoke/rotate the secret now** (assume it is compromised).
2. Check audit logs for its use; contain anything it touched.
3. Remove it from history: `git filter-repo --replace-text` + force-push; ask forks/clones to re-clone.
4. Move the secret to a vault (Key Vault, Secrets Manager) and the workflow to OIDC.
playbooks.prevent:
- gitleaks pre-commit + CI, GitHub push protection
- No long-lived cloud keys in CI: OIDC federation

playbooks.title: Critical CVE in a production image
playbooks.summary: The image scanner reports a Critical vulnerability in an image running in prod.
playbooks.symptoms: - Trivy/ECR/Defender alert: CRITICAL, fix available
playbooks.causes:
- Outdated base image or OS packages
- Vulnerable library version pinned in the app
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed <image>
trivy image --format json <image> | jq '.Results[].Vulnerabilities[]? | {id:.VulnerabilityID, pkg:.PkgName, fixed:.FixedVersion}' | head -40
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' | sort -u | grep <image-name>
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Check exploitability: internet-facing? in CISA KEV? high EPSS?
2. Bump the base image or package, rebuild, rescan (gate fails on Critical).
3. Deploy through the normal pipeline (canary), verify, roll back by tag if needed.
4. If no fix: mitigate (WAF rule, disable feature), document an expiring exception.
playbooks.prevent:
- Rebuild images weekly on fresh bases
- Continuous scanning of running images
- SBOMs to answer "where is this package?" in minutes

playbooks.title: Remove AWS keys from CI with OIDC
playbooks.summary: Your pipelines use long-lived AWS access keys stored as secrets. Replace them with short-lived OIDC credentials.
playbooks.symptoms:
- `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` secrets in CI
- Keys older than 90 days in IAM credential report
playbooks.causes: - Pipelines set up before OIDC support
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
aws iam generate-credential-report && aws iam get-credential-report --query Content --output text | base64 -d | cut -d, -f1,9,10,11 | column -ts,
aws iam list-open-id-connect-providers
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Create the OIDC provider `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` (audience `sts.amazonaws.com`).
2. Create a deploy role whose trust policy limits `sub` to `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main` (or an environment).
3. In the workflow: `permissions: id-token: write` and `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume`.
4. Delete the old keys; add an SCP to block new IAM user keys.
playbooks.prevent:
- One role per pipeline and environment, least privilege
- Same pattern for Azure (workload identity federation) and GCP

playbooks.title: Brute-force attempts on the login page
playbooks.summary: Thousands of failed logins per hour from many IPs.
playbooks.symptoms:
- Spike of POSTs to `/login` with 401/403
- Account lockouts, CPU up on the app
playbooks.causes: - Credential-stuffing bots
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
awk '$7 ~ /login/ && $9 ~ /40[13]/ {print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
sudo fail2ban-client status
```
playbooks.fix:
1. nginx `limit_req` on the login location (e.g. 5r/m per IP, 429).
2. Cloudflare/AWS WAF rate-based rule and bot challenge on `/login`.
3. MFA for users; lockout with backoff; captcha after failures.
4. fail2ban jail on repeated 401s for self-hosted.
playbooks.prevent:
- Alert on failed-login rate
- Breached-password checks at signup and login

playbooks.title: Harden SSH on a new server
playbooks.summary: A fresh VM with password SSH open to the internet.
playbooks.symptoms:
- `PasswordAuthentication yes`, root login allowed
- Thousands of `Failed password` lines in auth.log
playbooks.causes: - Default image settings
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
sudo sshd -T | grep -E 'passwordauthentication|permitrootlogin|pubkeyauthentication'
sudo grep -c 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log
```
playbooks.fix:
```bash
sudo sed -i 's/^#\?PasswordAuthentication.*/PasswordAuthentication no/; s/^#\?PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh   # keep your current session open!
sudo apt install -y fail2ban && sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH && sudo ufw enable
```
playbooks.prevent: - Restrict port 22 to known IPs or use SSM Session Manager / Tailscale instead of public SSH

playbooks.title: Everything runs in one availability zone
playbooks.summary: An AZ outage would take the whole product down.
playbooks.symptoms:
- All instances, the database and NAT in one subnet/AZ
- No failover tested
playbooks.causes: - Fast initial setup, cost savings, "we'll fix it later"
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,Placement.AvailabilityZone]' --output table
aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceIdentifier,MultiAZ,AvailabilityZone]'
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Spread the app tier over ≥2 AZs behind a load balancer (ASG/EKS node groups per AZ).
2. Database Multi-AZ (RDS/Aurora), cache with replicas.
3. NAT gateway per AZ (or VPC endpoints) so one AZ cannot cut egress.
4. Test: drain one AZ in a game day and measure.
playbooks.prevent:
- Architecture review checklist: no single points of failure
- Define RTO/RPO per service

playbooks.title: Should we split the monolith?
playbooks.summary: Teams step on each other and deploys are slow; someone proposes microservices.
playbooks.symptoms:
- One big deploy for every change
- Merge conflicts, long test suites
- One hot module needs more scale than the rest
playbooks.causes: - Unclear module boundaries, shared database tables
playbooks.diagnose: Map dependencies and change frequency per module; measure deploy lead time and failure rate (DORA).
playbooks.fix:
1. First make a **modular monolith**: clear module boundaries, no cross-module table access.
2. Extract only modules with a clear domain, independent scaling or release needs (strangler pattern, behind an API).
3. Have the platform ready first: CI/CD templates, observability, service discovery.
playbooks.prevent:
- ADRs for each split with expected benefits and costs
- Revisit with DORA metrics after each extraction

playbooks.title: Database falls over when the cache expires
playbooks.summary: Every few minutes the DB CPU spikes to 100% and latency explodes.
playbooks.symptoms:
- Periodic DB load spikes aligned with cache TTL
- Many identical queries at the same second
playbooks.causes: - Popular keys expire together; every request misses and hits the DB at once (thundering herd)
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'keyspace_(hits|misses)'
redis-cli --latency
# DB: top identical queries at spike times (slow log / performance_schema)
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Add jitter to TTLs.
2. Single-flight / lock so one request rebuilds a key while others wait or get stale data.
3. Refresh hot keys in the background before expiry.
4. Serve stale-while-revalidate.
playbooks.prevent:
- Alert on cache hit ratio drop
- Load test cache-cold scenarios

playbooks.title: No tested disaster recovery plan
playbooks.summary: Backups exist but nobody knows how long a full restore takes.
playbooks.symptoms:
- No RTO/RPO defined
- Last restore test: never
playbooks.causes: - DR treated as a checkbox
playbooks.diagnose: List every data store, its backup method, frequency, retention and where copies live (same account? same region?).
playbooks.fix:
1. Agree RPO/RTO per service with the business.
2. Pick a strategy per service (backup-restore, pilot light, warm standby).
3. Cross-region, cross-account, immutable backups.
4. Run a restore drill; write the runbook from what actually happened.
playbooks.prevent:
- Quarterly restore tests, timed
- IaC so the environment can be rebuilt

playbooks.title: Memory grows until the app is OOM-killed
playbooks.summary: The service's memory climbs steadily for hours, then the container restarts with OOMKilled.
playbooks.symptoms:
- RSS graph like a staircase
- `OOMKilled` / exit code 137 on restarts
playbooks.causes:
- Unbounded in-memory caches or lists
- Objects kept alive by global references, event listeners, closures
- Large responses buffered instead of streamed
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
kubectl -n prod top pod -l app=api
# Python
pip install memray && memray run app.py   # or tracemalloc snapshots
# Node
node --inspect app.js   # take heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools, compare
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Bound caches (LRU with max size, TTL).
2. Remove listeners/references when done; avoid module-level accumulators.
3. Stream large payloads.
4. Short term: `max-requests` worker recycling (gunicorn) while you fix it.
playbooks.prevent:
- Memory dashboards per version; alert on steady growth
- Load test for an hour, not five minutes

playbooks.title: API endpoint is slow (N+1 queries)
playbooks.summary: A list endpoint takes seconds and gets slower as data grows.
playbooks.symptoms:
- p95 grows with page size
- Hundreds of near-identical SQL queries per request
playbooks.causes:
- ORM lazy-loads related rows inside a loop (N+1)
- Missing index on the filter column
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
# Django: django-debug-toolbar / connection.queries; Rails: bullet; Frappe: frappe.db.sql log
# APM trace (Datadog/New Relic) shows the repeated span
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Fetch related data in one query (`select_related`/`prefetch_related`, joins, `IN (...)`).
2. Add the missing index.
3. Paginate, and select only needed columns.
playbooks.prevent:
- Query-count assertions in tests
- APM alerts on endpoint p95

playbooks.title: Tests pass locally but fail in CI
playbooks.summary: The same test fails randomly in the pipeline.
playbooks.symptoms:
- Re-run makes it green
- Fails more under parallel jobs
playbooks.causes:
- Order dependence or shared state between tests
- Time/timezone/locale assumptions
- Real network calls, sleeps and race conditions
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
pytest -p no:randomly -x            # then: pytest -p randomly --randomly-seed=<seed from CI>
pytest -n auto --count 20 tests/test_x.py   # pytest-repeat to reproduce
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Isolate state (fresh DB/transaction per test, no globals).
2. Freeze time (`freezegun`), fix timezone, mock the network.
3. Replace sleeps with explicit waits/conditions.
playbooks.prevent: - Quarantine and track flaky tests; don't just re-run

playbooks.title: Browser shows a CORS error
playbooks.summary: Frontend calls to the API fail with "blocked by CORS policy".
playbooks.symptoms:
- Works in curl/Postman, fails in browser
- Preflight OPTIONS returns 4xx or no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
playbooks.causes:
- API does not send CORS headers for that origin
- Proxy strips headers or does not answer OPTIONS
- Credentials used with `*` origin
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
curl -si -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/items -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' | head -20
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Allow the exact origin, methods and headers on the API (not `*` with credentials).
2. Make sure the proxy passes OPTIONS through and keeps the headers.
3. Or serve frontend and API from the same origin behind one proxy.
playbooks.prevent: - Keep allowed origins in config per environment

playbooks.title: Disk full, but du shows much less
playbooks.summary: `df` says 100% but `du` adds up to far less.
playbooks.symptoms:
- `No space left on device`
- `df -h` 100%, `du -sh /*` much smaller
playbooks.causes:
- Deleted files still held open by a process (usually logs)
- Inodes exhausted
- Data hidden under a mount point
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
df -h; df -i
sudo lsof +L1 | sort -k7 -n | tail          # deleted but open
sudo du -xh / --max-depth=2 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Restart the process holding the deleted file, or truncate it: `: > /proc/<pid>/fd/<fd>`.
2. For inodes, find and remove the millions of small files (sessions, cache).
3. Configure logrotate with `copytruncate` or a postrotate reload.
playbooks.prevent:
- Disk and inode alerts at 80%
- Log rotation for every service

playbooks.title: High load average but CPU is idle
playbooks.summary: Load is 12 on a 4-CPU box, yet `top` shows CPUs mostly idle.
playbooks.symptoms:
- High load, high `wa` (iowait) in top
- Processes in `D` state
playbooks.causes:
- Processes blocked on slow disk or NFS
- Saturated EBS volume (IOPS/throughput limit, burst credits gone)
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
vmstat 1 5
iostat -xz 1 5          # %util, await
ps -eo state,pid,cmd | awk '$1=="D"'
sudo iotop -oPa
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Find the process doing the I/O (iotop) and reduce it (batching, off-peak).
2. Move to faster storage (gp3 with more IOPS/throughput, local NVMe).
3. Fix hung NFS mounts (soft/timeo options, server health).
playbooks.prevent: - Alert on disk await and EBS burst balance

playbooks.title: systemd service fails to start
playbooks.summary: `systemctl start myapp` fails or the service keeps restarting.
playbooks.symptoms: - `Active: failed` or `activating (auto-restart)`
playbooks.causes: - Wrong path/user/permissions, missing env file, port already used, app crash on start
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
systemctl status myapp -l
journalctl -u myapp -b --no-pager | tail -50
systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
sudo ss -ltnp | grep :8000
sudo -u app /opt/myapp/venv/bin/gunicorn --check-config app:app
```
playbooks.fix: Fix what the journal shows (path, permissions, missing variable, port clash), then `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart myapp`.
playbooks.prevent:
- `Restart=on-failure` with `StartLimitBurst`
- Health check after deploys

playbooks.title: Clock drift breaks TLS and tokens
playbooks.summary: Random auth failures: JWT not yet valid, TLS certificate errors, cron at wrong times.
playbooks.symptoms: - `certificate is not yet valid`, `token used before issued`
playbooks.causes: - NTP not running or blocked; VM resumed after suspend
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
timedatectl
chronyc tracking
chronyc sources -v
```
playbooks.fix:
```bash
sudo apt install -y chrony && sudo systemctl enable --now chrony
sudo chronyc makestep
```
playbooks.prevent: - Monitor clock offset; use the cloud provider's time service

playbooks.title: "Too many open files" under load
playbooks.summary: Under traffic the service logs `EMFILE: too many open files`.
playbooks.symptoms: - Errors appear only at high concurrency
playbooks.causes: - Low `nofile` limit (1024 default) for the service; or a socket/file descriptor leak
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
cat /proc/$(pidof -s nginx)/limits | grep 'open files'
ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l
sysctl fs.file-max
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Raise the limit for the service: `LimitNOFILE=65535` in the systemd unit (or `worker_rlimit_nofile` in nginx).
2. If the count keeps growing, find the leak (unclosed files/sockets).
playbooks.prevent: - Alert on fd usage vs limit

playbooks.title: Read replica lag keeps growing
playbooks.summary: Replica is minutes behind the primary; users see stale data.
playbooks.symptoms:
- `Seconds_Behind_Source` growing
- Reads from replica miss recent writes
playbooks.causes:
- Large transactions or bulk updates on the primary
- Replica underpowered (I/O, CPU) or single-threaded apply
- Long-running queries on the replica blocking apply
playbooks.diagnose:
```sql
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
SHOW PROCESSLIST;
SELECT * FROM performance_schema.replication_applier_status_by_worker\G
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Break bulk jobs into small batches.
2. Enable parallel replication (`replica_parallel_workers`), scale the replica.
3. Kill or move long reports off the replica.
4. Route read-after-write paths to the primary.
playbooks.prevent:
- Alert on lag > 30 s
- Schedule batch jobs off-peak

playbooks.title: Deadlocks in production
playbooks.summary: The app logs `Deadlock found when trying to get lock`.
playbooks.symptoms: - Error 1213 bursts during busy periods
playbooks.causes:
- Two transactions lock the same rows in different orders
- Missing indexes make locks cover many rows
playbooks.diagnose:
```sql
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G   -- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section
SET GLOBAL innodb_print_all_deadlocks = ON;
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Access rows in a consistent order across code paths.
2. Keep transactions short; no user/network waits inside them.
3. Add indexes so updates lock fewer rows.
4. Retry deadlocked transactions in the app (they are safe to retry).
playbooks.prevent: - Log all deadlocks and review weekly

playbooks.title: "Too many connections"
playbooks.summary: New requests fail with `Too many connections` during traffic peaks.
playbooks.symptoms: - Error 1040 (MySQL) / `remaining connection slots are reserved` (PostgreSQL)
playbooks.causes:
- Every app instance opens its own big pool; autoscaling multiplies it
- Connections leaked or idle in transaction
playbooks.fix:
1. Size pools: (pods × pool size) < max_connections with headroom.
2. Put a pooler in front (ProxySQL, PgBouncer, RDS Proxy).
3. Fix leaks; set idle timeouts.
playbooks.prevent: - Alert at 80% of max_connections

playbooks.title: One query suddenly slow
playbooks.summary: A query that took 20 ms now takes 4 s.
playbooks.symptoms: - Slow query log entries, CPU up
playbooks.causes: - Plan changed (stats, data growth), missing index, implicit type conversion, function on the indexed column
playbooks.fix:
1. Add or fix the index for the WHERE/ORDER BY columns.
2. Avoid functions on indexed columns; match column types.
3. Refresh statistics.
playbooks.prevent: - Review slow log weekly; track top queries by total time

playbooks.title: Prove the backups actually restore
playbooks.summary: You have nightly dumps but never restored one.
playbooks.symptoms: - No documented restore time
playbooks.causes: - Restore testing not scheduled
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
mariadb-dump --single-transaction --routines --all-databases | gzip > /backup/all-$(date +%F).sql.gz
docker run -d --name restore-test -e MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=x mariadb:11.4
gunzip < /backup/all-$(date +%F).sql.gz | docker exec -i restore-test mariadb -uroot -px
```
playbooks.fix: Automate a weekly restore into a throwaway instance, run sanity queries (row counts, latest timestamps), record the duration as your real RTO.
playbooks.prevent: - Point-in-time recovery (binlogs/WAL) for RPO in minutes

playbooks.title: Cloud bill jumped this month
playbooks.summary: Spend is 40% higher than last month and nobody knows why.
playbooks.symptoms: - Budget alert, Cost Explorer spike
playbooks.causes:
- Forgotten resources (test clusters, big instances)
- NAT gateway / cross-AZ data transfer
- Logs ingestion explosion
- Autoscaling that never scaled down
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 --granularity DAILY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --query 'NatGateways[].NatGatewayId'
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Find the service and day where it jumped; drill by usage type and tag.
2. Stop or right-size the cause; add VPC endpoints for S3/ECR traffic.
3. Clean unattached volumes, idle load balancers, old snapshots.
playbooks.prevent: - Tags enforced (owner, env), budgets per team, anomaly detection

playbooks.title: EC2 instance unreachable
playbooks.summary: SSH and the app time out on an instance that was fine yesterday.
playbooks.symptoms:
- Connection timeout (not refused)
- Status checks failing or OK
playbooks.causes: - Security group / NACL change, route table change, instance out of memory, full disk, public IP changed after stop/start
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
aws ec2 describe-instance-status --instance-ids i-0abc --include-all-instances
aws ec2 get-console-output --instance-id i-0abc --latest | tail -50
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0abc --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions'
aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc     # works without SSH if SSM agent is up
```
playbooks.fix: Fix the network rule or route; if the OS is stuck, use the serial console or stop/start (note: public IP changes unless Elastic IP).
playbooks.prevent:
- Elastic IPs or a load balancer for stable endpoints
- CloudWatch alarms on status checks with auto-recover

playbooks.title: S3 bucket accidentally public
playbooks.summary: A bucket with private data is readable from the internet.
playbooks.symptoms:
- Security Hub / Macie / Trusted Advisor finding
- Objects open without credentials
playbooks.causes: - Bucket policy with `Principal: *`, ACLs, account-level block turned off
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket acme-data
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket acme-data
aws s3control get-public-access-block --account-id 123456789012
```
playbooks.fix:
```bash
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket acme-data --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
# then review access logs / CloudTrail data events for downloads during exposure
```
playbooks.prevent:
- Account-level Block Public Access + SCP to prevent turning it off
- Serve public files through CloudFront with OAC

playbooks.title: EKS pods stuck Pending
playbooks.summary: New pods stay Pending after a deploy or scale-up.
playbooks.symptoms: - `0/5 nodes are available: insufficient cpu` or `Too many pods`
playbooks.causes:
- No capacity and autoscaler not adding nodes
- ENI/IP limit per node (VPC CNI)
- Taints/affinity with no matching nodes
playbooks.diagnose:
```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod> | tail -20
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PODS:.status.allocatable.pods
kubectl -n karpenter logs deploy/karpenter | tail
```
playbooks.fix:
1. Fix Karpenter/cluster-autoscaler limits or node pool instance types.
2. Enable prefix delegation in VPC CNI for more pods per node.
3. Correct requests (too high?) and tolerations.
playbooks.prevent: - Alert on Pending pods > 5 min
